messages.subject: DLM for Proportions/Multinomial Model
parts:
Hello all,

I have a question that is more statistical that technical, so I apologize if this is not appropriate for the Stan list. I am wondering about how best to parameterize a dynamic linear model with a multinomial observation equation, where the parameters of interest are the time-specific population proportions for the different categories. The approach I've tried so far is to apply logit transformation to the proportions and specify the Gaussian DLM on that scale. Here is the code:

data {
    int<lower=1> T; // number of time periods
    int<lower=1> K; // number of categories
    int<lower=0> counts[T, K];
}
parameters {
    simplex[K] props[T]; // period-specific category proportions
    real<lower=0> tau; // innovation standard deviation
}
model {
    for (t in 1:T) {
        if (t > 1) {
            for (k in 1:K) {
                logit(props[t, k]) ~ normal(logit(props[t - 1, k]), tau); // Gaussian on logit scale
            }
        }
        counts[t] ~ multinomial(props[t]); // Multinomial sampling model
    }
}

This model seems to work well in the simulations I've run, but I am curious whether there is a better way to approach this problem. If not, I'll just stick with this. Thanks for your help!

Devin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] DLM for Proportions/Multinomial Model
parts:
I'll leave the statistical modeling advice to others, but
I'd like to point out that your model isn't quite correct as formulated.
The problem is that you need to add the Jacobian of the inverse
logit transform to the total log probability.

That'd be

for (k in 1:K) {
logit(props[t, k]) ~ normal(logit(props[t - 1, k]), tau); // Gaussian on logit scale

increment_log_prob(log(inv_logit(props[t,k])) + log1m(inv_logit(props[t,k])));
}

Here the Jacobian adjustment is the log of the derivative of the
inverse transform,

log | d/dp inv_logit(p) |

= log( inv_logit(p) * (1 - inv_logit(p) )

= log(inv_logit(p)) + log1m(inv_logit(p))

where p = props[t,k]. We discuss the Jacobian for the logit in the
section of the manual on constraints and transforms (near the end).

A more typical formulation I've seen is to parameterize props itself on the
logit scale (i.e., unconstrained vector[K] here), and then use softmax
to transform that to the parameter to plug into the multinomial. Then you
don't need to fiddle with Jacobians.

BUT, and this is a big but for now, our current softmax implementation has a memory
leak. If your system's small, it probably won't matter.
We fixed it on the 2.1.1 hotfix branch on GitHub, but we haven't released the
code with the fix yet, as we had the same kind of memory leak in a few other
functions that we're going to fix. In fact, I'm doing that in the other window
I have open now :-)

You could also speed the model up a bit by vectorizing the call to normal, but I'd
wait until the model's all working to try that.

- Bob

    simplex[K] props[T]; // period-specific category proportions
    real<lower=0> tau; // innovation standard deviation
}

transformed parameters {
    vector[K] logit_props[T]; // logit of proportions
for (t in 1:T) {
for (k in 1:K) {

logit_props[t, k] <- logit(props[t, k]);
            // Adjust for logit tranform by incrementing the log probability
            // by the log of the derivative of the inverse-logit
            increment_log_prob(log(inv_logit(props[t, k])) +
                               log1m(inv_logit(props[t, k])));

}
    }
}

    for (t in 1:T) {
        if (t > 1) {
logit_props[t] ~ normal(logit_props[t - 1], tau); //vectorized

}
        counts[t] ~ multinomial(props[t]);

data {

    int<lower=1> K; // number of categories
    int<lower=0> counts[T, K];

vector[K] logit_props[T]; // logit of proportions

real<lower=0> tau; // innovation standard deviation
}
transformed parameters {
simplex[K] props[T]; // period-specific category proportions
for (t in 1:T) {
props[t] <- softmax(logit_props[t]);

}
}
model {
    for (t in 1:T) {
        if (t > 1) {
logit_props[t] ~ normal(logit_props[t - 1], tau);

}
        counts[t] ~ multinomial(props[t]);
    }
}

Sorry --- I just realized I gave you the Jacobian the wrong way around.
I'm used to going from unconstrained parameters to parameters,
which involves the inverse logit. You're going the other way,
so you need to increment with the log absolute derivative of
the logits, not the inverse logits, that is:

log | d/dp logit(p) |

= log | d/dp log(p/(1-p)) |

= log | d/dp log(p) - d/dp log(1-p) |

= log | 1/p + 1/(1-p) |

= log ( 1/(p * (1-p)) )

= - log (p * (1 - p))

= -[log(p) + log(1-p)]

= -[log(p) + log1m(p)]

I'd check my work on that derivative, too.

- Bob

        }

counts[t] ~ multinomial(props[t]);
    }
}
Devin

parts: One more follow-up on this thread: Upon further reflection, I came to the conclusion that it would be more direct and possibly more efficient to use a Dirichlet distribution for the dynamic component of this model. I therefore re-wrote the model as follows:

data {
    int<lower=1> T; // number of time periods
    int<lower=1> K; // number of categories
    int<lower=0> counts[T, K];
}
parameters {
    simplex[K] props[T]; // period-specific category proportions
real<lower=1> priorN; // implied "sample size" of the previous period

}
model {
    for (t in 1:T) {
        if (t > 1) {
props[t] ~ dirichlet(priorN * props[t - 1]); // transition equation

}
        counts[t] ~ multinomial(props[t]);
    }
}

Note that the parameter "priorN" plays roughly the same role as the innovation standard deviation parameter "tau" in the earlier version of the model.

~Devin

Neat. Did it work as expected?

Both these models remind me of Blei and Lafferty's dynamic topic models, which are
also time-series multinomials, although modeled quite differently:
